spec.title: The compliance package a machine can refuse
spec.intro:
Module 10's crosswalk was a table a human reads; this workspace holds the same idea as
documents a machine can refuse. It is staged exactly as `bash labs/setup.sh ./lab12`
leaves it: a minimal OSCAL catalog (the spine as data), a profile that selects from it,
a component-definition that links control `ac-2` to the Module-09 policy that enforces
it, a deliberately broken catalog, and the validator's own source. The "Run validator"
button IS the pipeline's validate step — it runs the committed `validate-oscal.ts`
logic, verified byte-for-byte in CI against real `bun` runs of that script, so every
verdict and exit code you see here is the one a real machine produces. The pipeline
reads the catalog at a fixed path, `lab12/catalog-under-validation.json` — seeded with
your good catalog, exactly like a CI checkout — while the pristine fixtures stay
untouched beside it. One more thing to notice while you trace: the spine also defines
`sc-28`, protection of information at rest — the laptop-encryption claim this
curriculum keeps re-asking — and this SOC 2 profile doesn't select it. Selection is a
decision, and now it's data.

tasks.instruction:
Before running anything, open `lab12/acme-catalog.json` and find the three pieces
the schema requires for this document to be a catalog at all: the document UUID,
the metadata that names and versions it, and controls with stable ids. Record each
in section 1 of `lab12/oscal-worksheet.md`, copying the values exactly as the file
holds them.

hints.nudge: Three layers of identity: the `uuid` names THIS document, `metadata` names and versions the catalog, and each control's `id` is the handle everything later points at.

hints.concept: §4.2 — the catalog: your spine, as data; absence of a required piece is the violation

hints.reveal: document-uuid: 11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111 · metadata-title: Acme Internal Control Spine · control-ids: ac-2, sc-28

tasks.explain:
Module 10's crosswalk cell `AC-2` is now an addressable object with a document UUID
above it and a stable id on it. None of it is decoration: a control with no `id`
isn't "incomplete" — nothing can reference it, so the document fails the schema's
contract entirely. That distinction is the whole module.

tasks.instruction:
Open `lab12/acme-profile.json`. It copies no controls — it imports a catalog and
declares a selection. In section 2 of the worksheet, record which catalog it
imports, which control ids it puts in scope, and which control the catalog defines
that this profile does NOT select.

hints.nudge: Look inside `imports`: the `href` names the catalog, `with-ids` lists the selection. Then compare that list against the catalog's two control ids — what's left out?

hints.concept: §4.3 — a profile is a selection over a catalog: Module 10's 'a framework is a subset of the spine', made mechanical

hints.reveal: imports-href: acme-catalog.json · in-scope-ids: ac-2 · defined-but-not-selected: sc-28

tasks.explain:
The profile is the crosswalk's "SOC 2 cares about these spine controls" as data —
change the include-list, change the framework's scope, in a diffable file. And the
control it leaves out is `sc-28`, the encryption-at-rest claim this curriculum has
chased since module 01: defined in the spine, out of scope for this framework.
That gap being visible in data, not in someone's memory, is the point.

tasks.instruction:
Open `lab12/acme-component.json` and trace the C2P join that makes this more than
format conversion: the implemented requirement's `control-id`, the `links` entry
whose `rel` is `policy`, and the `back-matter` resource its `href` resolves to.
Record all three in section 3 of the worksheet. The policy id you land on is the
Module-09 policy-as-code rule that denies `legacy-admin` grants in CI.

hints.nudge: Walk it in order: `implemented-requirements[0].control-id` → its `links[0].href` → the back-matter resource whose `policy-id` prop the href names.

hints.concept: §4.6 — C2P links the OSCAL claim to the enforcing code, by identifier, in a field a machine can follow

tasks.explain:
You just followed the chain a machine follows: the profile put `ac-2` in scope, the
component claims `ac-2` is implemented, and the claim carries — as data — the
identifier of the Module-09 policy that enforces it. The document doesn't just say
"implemented"; it says "implemented by THIS, provably". That link is the difference
between asserting a control and wiring the assertion to the enforcement.

tasks.instruction:
Run the validator: click "Run validator" — the pipeline's validate step over the
staged set. Confirm the verdict is PASS with exit code 0, that the profile resolves
with zero dangling references, and that `ac-2` is policy-linked. Then keep the
verdict: copy the validator's complete output into
`lab12/oscal-validation-pass.txt`, replacing the placeholder line.

verify.stdout_matches: ^PASS: required fields present, profile references resolve, control is implemented and policy-linked$

hints.nudge: Run validator IS `bun validate-oscal.ts` over the three staged documents. Watch the exit code under the output — 0 is the machine's blessing. The record itself is evidence: keep all of it.

hints.concept: §4.7 — the validator makes the schema bite; its verdict is an exit code because the consumer is a CI pipeline

hints.reveal: Click Run validator (PASS, exit 0), then copy its full output into lab12/oscal-validation-pass.txt in place of the placeholder line

tasks.explain:
A machine just judged the whole package — required fields present, every profile
reference resolved, the implemented control wired to its policy — and blessed it
with exit 0, no human reading required. The record you kept is the §6 deliverable:
the EVALUATE verdict frozen as a file, produced by the gate itself, so it cannot
drift from what the gate actually checked.

tasks.instruction:
Now make the gate bite. Replace the ENTIRE contents of
`lab12/catalog-under-validation.json` with `lab12/acme-catalog-broken.json`'s
contents (copy the whole file) — the same catalog with one control's `id` removed —
and run the validator. Confirm it fails with exit code 1, naming the missing field
AND the downstream consumer the defect would break. Copy the complete FAIL record
into `lab12/oscal-broken-record.txt`, record the diagnosis in section 4 of the
worksheet, then restore the set: copy `lab12/acme-catalog.json` back over
`lab12/catalog-under-validation.json`.

verify.regex: ^  -> a control with no id cannot be referenced by a profile or a policy link; this would break any importer \(an auditor's tool, a FedRAMP pipeline\) downstream\.$

hints.nudge: Swap the broken catalog into the slot the pipeline reads (select all, copy, paste), run, and read the FAIL record like an auditor: it names the field AND who downstream it breaks. Don't leave the working tree red — restore the good catalog after.

hints.concept: §4.7 — a failing exit names the field that broke and the consumer it would have broken; §5.4 — the verdict, the way a machine reports it

hints.reveal: Copy lab12/acme-catalog-broken.json over lab12/catalog-under-validation.json, Run validator (FAIL, exit 1), copy the output into lab12/oscal-broken-record.txt, fill worksheet section 4 (missing-required-field: id · downstream-consumer-broken: any importer — an auditor's tool, a FedRAMP pipeline), then copy lab12/acme-catalog.json back over lab12/catalog-under-validation.json

tasks.explain:
The defect was one missing field, and the blast radius was named for you: a control
with no `id` can't be referenced by the profile, the implementation, or the policy
link, so any importer downstream — an auditor's tool, a FedRAMP pipeline — chokes
on it. Catching that in CI, with the consumer spelled out, is the difference
between a malformed audit package failing a build and shipping to an assessor.

tasks.instruction:
Break a different thing yourself. Edit `lab12/acme-profile.json` so its `with-ids`
selects `ac-9` — a control id the catalog does not define — and run the validator.
Confirm it flags the dangling reference with exit 1 and copy the complete FAIL
record into `lab12/oscal-dangling-record.txt`. Then restore the profile to select
`ac-2` again and re-run the validator until the set is green.

verify.regex: ^FAIL: profile references control id\(s\) the catalog does not define: ac-9$

verify.stdout_matches: ^PASS: required fields present, profile references resolve, control is implemented and policy-linked$

hints.nudge: One token in `with-ids` is the whole edit. The catalog defines ac-2 and sc-28 — ac-9 has no home in the spine, so the selection can't resolve. Remember the cycle isn't done at the FAIL: restore, re-run, leave it green.

hints.concept: §4.3 — a profile including an id the catalog doesn't define is the OSCAL form of a Module-10 crosswalk orphan

hints.reveal: Edit lab12/acme-profile.json: "ac-2" → "ac-9" in with-ids, Run validator (FAIL, exit 1), copy the output into lab12/oscal-dangling-record.txt, edit "ac-9" back to "ac-2", Run validator again (PASS, exit 0)

tasks.explain:
That FAIL is the Module-10 orphan check, mechanized: the profile claimed a control
with no home in the spine, and a resolving validator refused the document instead
of trusting your eyes to spot it. You also just practiced the full discipline —
break, observe the named defect, restore, re-run to green — which is exactly what
a CI pipeline demands of an author whose change is blocked.

tasks.instruction:
The real §6 task 7 runs on your own machine: install compliance-trestle, import
this lab's catalog, and validate it against the actual OSCAL schema. Before (or
instead of) doing that, answer in 2–4 sentences: which repository is the maintained
home of trestle, and why is pointing your toolchain at the dead NIST-hosted one a
defect and not a footnote? And name the kind of field the real schema requires that
this lab's minimal fixtures omit — the delta §4.8 calls Tier-C volatility.

hints.nudge: §4.8 names both: the maintained oscal-compass home vs the dead usnistgov repo, and the real schema's heavier requirements (more UUIDs, last-modified, parties/roles in metadata).

hints.concept: §4.8 — a tool's current home and current status are part of its correctness

tasks.instruction:
The lab's written deliverable, in 4–6 sentences for a colleague who keeps controls
in a spreadsheet: what a schema gives you that a shared format does not (use the
no-`id` control as the example — why it's invalid, not incomplete); what each layer
you touched is the machine-readable version of; the `ac-2` chain from profile to
implementation to enforcing policy, in words; and which downstream consumer the
broken catalog would have hurt, and how the dangling `ac-9` is Module 10's
crosswalk orphan wearing a schema.

hints.nudge: Walk §3's six parts in order: schema → catalog → profile → component-definition → C2P link → validator. The package stops being files a human mentally joins and becomes one validatable graph.

hints.concept: §3 — The Mental Model: why isn't a shared file format enough?

# Lab 12 worksheet — the OSCAL set, traced before it is trusted

Fill each answer on its own line, keeping the line's leading label exactly as
shown. Your sources are the staged JSON documents and the validator's own
records — this worksheet is reconciliation, not memory.

## 1. The three pieces a valid catalog requires
Open acme-catalog.json and copy each value exactly as the file holds it
(for control-ids, list every control id the catalog defines, in order):

document-uuid:
metadata-title:
control-ids:

## 2. The profile is a selection over the catalog
Open acme-profile.json. Which catalog does it import, which control ids does
it put in scope — and which control does the catalog define that this
profile does NOT select?

imports-href:
in-scope-ids:
defined-but-not-selected:

## 3. The C2P chain, traced by identifier
Open acme-component.json and walk the join: the implemented requirement's
control id, the policy link's href, and the back-matter policy id that
href resolves to.

chain-control-id:
chain-link-href:
chain-policy-id:

## 4. The broken catalog, diagnosed
From the FAIL record you captured (oscal-broken-record.txt): the missing
required field, and the downstream consumer the validator says the defect
would break.

missing-required-field:
downstream-consumer-broken:
